Married for 12 years, with two children aged 6 and 9. I was 30 when we had our first child, and my partner was 33. She wanted children, believing there was more to life. I grew up in a large family and always thought I would have kids, but I never felt ready. I realized I would never feel completely ready and that I wanted them, so it seemed like as good a time as any.

The first year was amazing. I reduced my work to four days a week, dedicating one solid day to caring for the baby, and it was fantastic. The second year brought major depression as work burned me out and the child didn't sleep well. By the third year, our second child arrived. At that point, I realized that while I thought it was hard with one child, I had no idea how challenging it would be with two. I've heard that three is even harder, but with four or more, you get the hang of it, and it becomes easier. Regardless, I decided that having three would be too expensive since we enjoy being able to afford vacations.

I have to say, having children is a blast. It's hard work. They require time, energy, and money. Every Saturday and Sunday morning is spent taking the kids to their various commitments. Additionally, twice a week in the evenings, one of us is out of the house until late taking our daughter to her dance class. Spare time and spare money are effectively nonexistent. (Looking back, I realize they don't drain all our finances. While I’m not buying a new computer every year, we do manage to take a couple of week-long road trips each year and fly back to visit family at least every other year.)

But I absolutely love it. Watching them form their own observations about the world is fantastic, and seeing them develop their own understanding of how things work is a true delight.

It's challenging listening to my daughter chatter away. She creates the most imaginative stories and talks for hours, much to my annoyance, even taking her books into the bathroom. My son has a more analytical mind. My partner often works late in a higher-paying executive role or travels for business, but the kids pull together, and we run the household like a well-oiled machine.

There’s chaos and laughter. There are tears and smiles.

It is both that difficult and that wonderful. With children, the range of life experiences expands. You lose time, but you gain joy. You lose the luxury of being self-centered, but you gain a profound understanding that you would do anything for them. They teach you a new dimension of love and bring another level of happiness. You know that your decisions will now involve a lot of compromise, but others will be thinking of you.

I guess what I'm trying to say is this: they change your life, they don’t end it. How you adapt to that change will define your journey as a parent.

Good luck! :)

To clarify - the sync speed (which is the speed at which the modem can communicate with the digital subscriber line access multiplexer in the exchange) is a function of the quality of the copper phone line.

Then there's throughput which is a function of congestion and/or rate limiting of the data flowing across the link. (e.g. your internet service provider has limited backhaul to the exchange, so your throughput is slowed down; the web server you're downloading from has a poor connection, so it can't send data to you as fast as your connection can handle it; your internet service provider has edge routers which rate limit peer-to-peer traffic; ...and so on.)

When you increment a pointer, you move it to the next memory location based on the size of the data type it points to.
